newsitem.title: JAPAN: JR West reaps modest profits, but faces hurdles.
newsitem.headline: JR West reaps modest profits, but faces hurdles.

text.p: West Japan Railway Co (JR West) announced modest profit growth in its first earnings report since it went public in October, but analysts warned that the former state-owned firm faces some hurdles.
The firm said on Wednesday that its current profit for the first half to September 30 rose 8.6 percent to 37.94 billion yen ($338 million).
At the same time, however, it announced a painful restructuring programme -- a cut of more than 25 percent in its workforce, which currently totals 47,000, over the next 10 years.

The company said the growth in earnings was led by higher profits from JR's super-fast bullet train services, with passenger numbers rising back to where they were before a killer earthquake devastated western Japan in January 1995.
"We've overcome the damage caused by last year's Kobe earthquake," a company official told reporters.
JR West's service area includes the Osaka and Kobe districts, the commercial hub of western Japan.

The company was born of the splitting up of the former Japan National Railways in 1987. JR West and East Japan Railway Co, the two biggest, are the only members of the seven-company JR group which are listed.
JR East, which was listed three years ago, said its first-half profits slipped 3.3 percent to 65.94 billion yen ($588 million).

Analysts said the results were no surprise and were unlikely cause any immediate movement in the two companies' shares. The results were announced after the Tokyo stock market had finished trading for the day.
JR West ended 1,000 yen lower at 373,000 yen and JR East fell 1,000 yen to 525,000 yen.
Both firms expect full-year profits to be largely unchanged from the previous year.
But JR West said costs for early retirement programmes and for repairing trains were likely to pressure its profits.
It forecast a 55 billion yen ($491 million) current profit, compared with 55.62 billion yen ($496 million) last business year.
JR East expects 103 billion yen ($919 million) current profit for the full year, largely unchanged.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.
Some analysts said debt left by the former Japan National Railways (JNR) was overshadowing the outlook for JR group firms.
A settlement body set up by the government took over 25.5 trillion yen ($227 billion) worth of the heavily indebted JNR's debt when the railway was split up.
The government had hoped to deal with the debt by selling land left by JNR and the state-owned shares of JR firms, but this has been delayed while the interest on the debt has burgeoned.

The government has not yet come up with any solution to the snowballing railway debt, but some politicians have hinted that the JR companies may have to shoulder some of it. Analysts say this might force the railways to raise fares.
Analysts said the fact that the bulk of JR group shares remained unsold could spark oversupply fears in the stock market.
JR West has sold 1.37 million shares on the market out of the two million it has already issued. It plans to sell the remaining shares next year at the earliest. ($1=112 yen)
